editorial.question: Which important RAN1 and RAN4 choices are advancing, and what dependencies remain?
editorial.answer: Access for narrowband devices, network sleep, filter removal, measurement scheduling, model interoperability and satellite operation enter the Calgary discussions together.
editorial.mechanism: Control and system-information resources must be decodable before a device can report its capabilities.; The sleeping network must receive a request and transmit a response; the device must obtain configuration and wait.; Oscillator position and resource allocation change distortion products and protected-band exposure.; Lost control and feedback affect subsequent scheduling and link adaptation.; Encoder and decoder assumptions must match; evaluation channels must preserve the correlations used for prediction.; Feeder-link compensation and moving multi-beam interference have different network and device dependencies.
editorial.tradeoff: Wider resources versus access by lower-bandwidth devices.; Access latency versus network and device energy.; Less filtering versus power back-off and retuning interruptions.; Device autonomy versus network scheduling visibility.; Configuration detail versus signaling overhead and generalization.; Device processing simplicity versus explicit deployment assumptions.
editorial.consequence: Evaluate coverage with the lowest-tier device included.; Separate request-specific gains from gains available through sparse periodic operation.; Test allocation, retuning and receiver blocking together.; Compare timing visibility with realistic feedback and traffic.; Verify compatibility metadata and cross-deployment evaluation before claiming measurement savings.; State the compensation reference and victim geometry before comparing results.
editorial.novelty: Restores meeting-wide analysis across independent areas, distinguishing company positions from recorded replies and linking algorithm, protocol and radio constraints.
editorial.uncertainty: This is a pre-meeting survey; no Calgary company proposal is presented as adopted.; Complete channel-coding, sensing and Release-20 work-item coverage is deferred rather than inferred from titles.; Numerical results are attributed to their company evaluation and are not pooled across different assumptions.
editorial.analysis_excerpt: RAN1's compensation design and RAN4's protection study therefore need explicit deployment descriptions before their results can be combined. A device-frequency-error assumption does not define the distribution of aggregate interference, and a coexistence loss metric does not specify how the device obtains timing. The Calgary agenda has to preserve those separate dependencies while deciding which assumptions belong in common requirements and which remain implementation choices.

topics.analysis_excerpt: The decisions should be judged together. A wider control region may help one coverage condition while additional configuration bits or a wider minimum receiver burden another. A gain measured only for a wideband receiver would leave the initial-access question unanswered.

topics.heading: A wake-up request can spend the energy that sleep saves
topics.finding: Wake-up benefit depends on the baseline and use case.
topics.mechanism: The sleeping network must receive a request and transmit a response; the device must obtain configuration and wait.

topics.analysis_excerpt: The access and sleep discussions consequently share a prerequisite: the device needs enough timing and configuration to request the signals it lacks. A standalone cell that transmits nothing before the request creates a different feasibility problem from an assisted carrier. The next evaluation should preserve those deployment differences and compare the request against a practical sparse periodic baseline, with both network and device energy included.

topics.heading: Removing a filter can give the scheduler a new constraint
topics.finding: Filterless radio operation may need implementation-aware scheduling.
topics.mechanism: Oscillator position and resource allocation change distortion products and protected-band exposure.
topics.tradeoff: Less filtering versus power back-off and retuning interruptions.
topics.next_step: Test allocation, retuning and receiver blocking together.
topics.analysis_excerpt: These are separate proposals, but they constrain the same act of scheduling a transmission. A filterless device may need a restricted allocation or a retuning guard; a shared-spectrum deployment may restrict where that allocation can move. Assessing component savings in isolation would miss the network information and scheduling freedom needed to realize them. Receiver blocking remains an additional check, not something a transmitter back-off calculation resolves.

topics.heading: The scheduler needs to know when the receiver is absent
topics.finding: Interruption duration alone does not predict throughput.
topics.mechanism: Lost control and feedback affect subsequent scheduling and link adaptation.
topics.tradeoff: Device autonomy versus network scheduling visibility.
topics.next_step: Compare timing visibility with realistic feedback and traffic.
topics.analysis_excerpt: This connects directly to oscillator retuning in filterless designs, without making the two procedures identical. In each case, an implementation-level transition can create a scheduling-visible absence. The relevant contract is what the network knows about affected carriers and timing, and how its feedback handling responds. Reporting only the fraction of receiver time lost would not capture those dependencies.

topics.heading: A learned radio function needs a compatibility contract
topics.finding: Model interoperability and reproducible prediction are separate prerequisites.
topics.mechanism: Encoder and decoder assumptions must match; evaluation channels must preserve the correlations used for prediction.
topics.tradeoff: Configuration detail versus signaling overhead and generalization.
topics.next_step: Verify compatibility metadata and cross-deployment evaluation before claiming measurement savings.
topics.analysis_excerpt: The connection is not that both tasks need the same model. Both need a stated boundary between what is exchanged or assumed and what performance is promised. Compression needs an encoder that the intended decoder can use. Measurement prediction needs a channel relationship that survives the evaluation conditions. An attractive accuracy result in a matched setup does not establish either interoperability across implementations or generalization across deployments.

claims.claim: The Calgary agenda reaches from the first information a device must decode to the radio components it can leave out. Radio Access Network Working Group 1 (RAN1) is considering broader control resources, simpler bandwidth signaling and requests that wake a sleeping network. Radio Access Network Working Group 4 (RAN4) has to determine how much of that flexibility survives transmitter constraints, receiver interruptions and reproducible testing. Several of these proposals reduce one burden by placing a new condition on access, scheduling or testing.

claims.claim: A cell cannot rely on a device's later capability report to fix an initial-access format that the device cannot receive. Apple's downlink-control paper applies that constraint to the physical downlink control channel (PDCCH) scheduling the first system-information block (SIB1). It argues that a control resource set wider than the smallest maximum bandwidth of low-tier devices would prevent those devices accessing the cell, even if the wider transmission improved coverage for other equipment.

claims.claim: Apple's bandwidth paper questions whether 6G should retain the explicit common-grid offset used by New Radio (NR). It reports that the corresponding offset is rarely nonzero in its observed deployments and proposes making the first resource block of a single carrier the common-grid origin. Its motivation includes reducing mandatory SIB1 signaling. This is a proposal to remove a configuration degree of freedom, based on deployment evidence, rather than a claim that all legacy grid rules can simply disappear.

claims.claim: An uplink wake-up signal lets a device request activity that a sleeping network has stopped providing continuously. The cost is a receiving path that listens for requests, device transmission and response monitoring, and the means to deliver the request configuration. Samsung therefore asks whether the additional energy-saving gain comes from the request itself or from a sparse broadcast configuration that would also work without it.
claims.passage: The main motivation of UL WUS is to enable UE-triggered on-demand requests for NES-related BS operation, so that UE performance degradation arising from NES operation can be compensated without sacrificing the NES gain. Under NES operation, transmission of DL common signals may be extended or suspended for BS power saving, which may degrade UE performance.

claims.passage: The NES gain attributable to UL WUS depends on the baseline configuration and evaluation assumptions. In particular, sparse SSB transmission, longer SIB1 periodicity and reduced-TRxRU reception can provide NES gain without UL WUS. When these effects are separated, the additional NES gain of UL WUS is limited or negative for most evaluated use cases.

claims.claim: One of Samsung's evaluated cases makes the baseline issue concrete. Compared with a 20-millisecond SIB1 baseline, it attributes 28 percentage points of a 30.1% no-request network-energy gain to extending periodic SIB1 transmission to 160 milliseconds. Those savings cannot all be credited to wake-up signaling. In a different synchronization-adaptation case, the request reduces modeled access latency from 246.5 to 50.5 milliseconds, but consumes additional network and device energy. The two results describe distinct use cases, not one combined operating point.
claims.passage: For UE-initiated on-demand SIB1 in DS#1b, compared with the baseline with 20 ms SIB1, 28.0 percentage points of the 30.1% NES gain (Cat1, without request) can already be obtained by changing the SIB1 periodicity to 160 ms without UL WUS.

claims.passage: For UE performance, UL WUS reduces the access latency from 246.5 ms to 50.5 ms under the assumption that two SSB bursts are needed for synchronization. This shows that UL WUS can mitigate the access latency increase caused by sparse SSB transmission. However, the latency benefit depends on the assumed synchronization procedure and the number of SSB bursts required by the UE. In addition, the UE energy saving gain is -0.3% at 2% access probability per I-DRX cycle.

claims.claim: The surface-acoustic-wave (SAW) filter discussion is about more than the minimum channel bandwidth. Removing filtering changes the protection offered to nearby bands and to the receiver. Nokia asks that a device be able to report implementation-specific uplink allocation restrictions and required power back-off. It argues that one worst-case back-off value across implementations could force the network to schedule every device against the most restrictive case.
claims.passage: The Hybrid approach was proposed to allow additional power backoff for UL BW/RB allocation at a frequency edge of an operating edge where the protected band is close in the frequency domain. However, the current approach of specifying additional power backoff values (in terms of ∆MPR or A-MPR) means that the specified values would likely be the maximum required power backoff values among different UE implementations of all vendors participating in the discussion. Consequently, the NW needs to consider the maximum allowed power backoff among different UE implementations with SAW-less design when configuring the UL BW/RB allocation for each UE connection.

claims.passage: In WF[1], there is FFS on LO position and LO retuning granularity. In our opinion, LO retuning granularity and LO position needs to discuss together. If the LO would be retuned to centre of the RB allocation, the needed LO granularity can be one RB, but if the LO would be placed at centre of the a RB region with a larger RB allocation size, e.g. 20 RB, LO retuning may not be needed very often, only between the different RB regions and therefore a coarse LO retuning granularity will be possible. Coarser LO retuning granularity would be helpful to reduce the need of guard time but at a cost of higher back off power. In summary, dividing the RB allocation into several RB allocation regions where a fixed LO position within each RB region is a more feasible solution for non-transparent LO retuning scheme.

claims.claim: Apple's multi-radio-access-technology spectrum-sharing paper shows why the freedom to move resources is limited by existing deployments. Aligning 5G and 6G resource grids can require changing carrier positions or existing aggregated-carrier arrangements. Apple identifies license-block edges as a constraint and asks operators about the feasibility of adjusting existing carrier-aggregation positions. Its proposed synchronization-raster simplification also has to preserve alignment where the generations share spectrum.
claims.passage: It seems relatively easier to accommodate this scenario as the RB alignment can be done either via shifting the center frequency of 5G carrier to different channel raster or shifting the center frequency of 6G carrier to different channel raster. One issue to be addressed is that if the grid shifting results in over spilling of operator’s spectrum license and some solutions are needed to address the potential interference issue to adjacent service or operator.

Apple identifies license-block edges as a constraint and asks operators about the feasibility of adjusting existing carrier-aggregation positions. Its proposed synchronization-raster simplification also has to preserve alignment where the generations share spectrum.
claims.passage: In 5G CA, the channel spacing for intra-band contiguous carrier aggregation can be adjusted to any multiple of least common multiple of channel raster, the enhanced channel raster if supported, and sub-carrier spacing less than the nominal channel spacing to optimize performance in a particular deployment scenario. There is no specification requirement to ensure one carrier’s RB grid to be aligned with another one’s. To ensure RB boundary alignment between 5G CA CCs and 6G single CC with large CBW, 5G CA component CC position in the field  might need to be adjusted. Given the SCC is configured via dedicated RRC signaling after the primary CC connection is established, which means the adjustment is feasible from specification perspective. The issue left is whether the adjustment is feasible from existing network deployment perspective. Operator/network vendor input is needed to understand the effort and interest to do so at first.

claims.claim: The measurement-gap debate asks how much freedom a device should have to retune its receiver while remaining connected. Nokia reports that its practical link adaptation treats interruption-related failures as evidence of poor channel conditions. The resulting reduction in transmission rate can persist beyond the short interruption. Its simulations also examine how an interrupted initial transmission can harm later retransmissions through the accumulated decoding state.
claims.passage: Observation 5: S1-O1 and S1-O2 throughput loss is largely explained by MCS shift caused by OLLA not able to distinguish between interruptions and errors caused by channel conditions.

claims.passage: In AI-RRM Sub-case 2, the AI/ML model is trained to predict L3 cell-level measurements of non-collocated cell(s) on a target frequency layer, which are not on the same site as measured cell(s). The cross-site correlation learned by the model is determined by the channel model realization used for training, e.g., cross-site correlation. If the model is insufficiently generalized, it may perform well only for the realization it was trained on and degrade under different realizations, deployments, or UE speeds. This may lead to frequent model switching or fallback to legacy measurements, thereby losing the expected gains. Therefore, RAN4 should consider generalization aspects when selecting channel model for AI RRM Sub-case 2.

claims.claim: Non-terrestrial network (NTN) proposals reach beyond extending terrestrial coverage. Apple supports full network pre-compensation of feeder-link Doppler for a transparent satellite payload. Its argument is that residual feeder-link effects can increase the frequency error a device must handle, while coupling uplink frequency correction to timing-drift parameters can introduce quantization error into the frequency loop. This places the correction at a specific part of the link rather than treating all observed frequency error as a device problem.
claims.passage: In a transparent payload case, how the network pre-compensates the feeder link Doppler remains an open issue. In Alternative 1, the feeder link Doppler is fully pre-compensated by the network. In Alternative 2, the feeder link Doppler is pre-compensated by the network in a way that, over the downlink on the service link, the observed time drift rate matches the observed frequency error. In our view, Alternative 1 should be supported for the following reasons:
